title: Search a 2D Matrix II
pattern: rank of a value in row-major sorted order / single counting pass over the grid
statement:
`matrix` holds integers in any order: `R` rows and `C` columns, every row the same length. Searching it means first placing its values in non-decreasing order, filling the first row from left to right, then the second row, and so on. That layout puts the smallest value in the top-left cell, keeps every row non-decreasing, keeps every column non-decreasing, and gives every copy of a value one fixed cell.

Return `[row, col]`, the cell holding the first copy of `target` in that layout, or `[-1, -1]` when no value equals `target`.

For example `matrix = [[3, 1], [4, 2]]` with `target = 3`: the values in order are `1, 2, 3, 4` and the layout is `[[1, 2], [3, 4]]`, so `3` sits at row 1, column 0 and the answer is `[1, 0]`. The same grid with `target = 5` gives `[-1, -1]`.

Constraints: `1 <= matrix.length <= 100`, `1 <= matrix[0].length <= 100`, `-100 <= matrix[i][j] <= 100` and `-100 <= target <= 100`.

constraints: Function signature: `function solve(matrix: number[][], target: number)`.
Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: Ask what a single cell of the ordered layout needs to know: only how many values are smaller than the value that belongs there.

The first copy of the target takes exactly the position equal to the number of values strictly smaller than it, so one pass that counts them answers the question and the ordered grid never has to be built.
Convert that flat position with the column count: `rank / C` is the row and `rank % C` is the column. If no cell equals the target, answer `[-1, -1]`.

editorial.approach: The brute force learns the position of every copy of the target separately: for each cell that holds the target it walks the whole grid to count how many values are smaller, and how many equal values are read before that cell, which is the rank the copy takes once the values are laid out in order. One full grid scan per accepted occurrence makes that O((R·C)²), which is quadratic on a grid full of copies of the target. The optimal notices that the first copy of a value always takes exactly the position equal to the number of values strictly smaller than it, so the whole layout never has to be built: a single pass gathers that count plus one flag for whether the target occurs at all, and the flat position becomes a row and a column through a division and a remainder, in O(R·C) time and O(1) extra space.
editorial.why_optimal: Reporting the position of a value needs the length of the block of values below it, and every cell the pass has not looked at could belong to that block, so Ω(R·C) is a floor and the single counting pass reaches it without sorting anything or copying the grid. The brute force meets that same floor once per accepted occurrence, and that is the factor the one-pass count removes: with `R·C` at most 10,000 either version is instant, so the point of the linear pass is what it refuses to do, not the stopwatch. The division is load-bearing: the flat rank turns into `row = rank / C` and `col = rank % C` with the column count, so a non-square grid exposes a wrong divisor immediately.
editorial.pitfalls: Dividing by the row count instead of the column count when converting the flat rank into `[row, col]`, which lands on a wrong cell on every non-square grid. Counting the equal values as smaller than the target, which pushes the answer right by one position for each earlier copy. Reporting the last copy rather than the first: the first copy sits exactly at the number of strictly smaller values. Returning `[0, 0]` instead of `[-1, -1]` when the target is absent, because a zero count of smaller values is not the same thing as a find. And reading `matrix[0]` without checking that the grid has a row at all.
